title: Checkpoint: Distributed Systems
subtitle: Reason across observability, overload, consistency, partitions, consensus, and recovery
objectives: Recall observability, resilience, consistency, CAP, consensus, and recovery without the unit label as a cue
Tell the difference between a real guarantee and a plausible sentence about one
Diagnose a distributed failure where the obvious fix is the bug

exercises.prompt: A retried order can publish the same fulfillment message twice. Make the consumer record the message ID atomically with its state change.
exercises.afterStatus: REDELIVERY · existing message ID found · inventory unchanged
exercises.result: At-least-once delivery produced one business effect
exercises.why: A unique message ID recorded in the same transaction as the inventory update lets redelivery detect a completed effect. A separate check-then-update sequence can race and apply the effect twice.

Place Worker, Inventory + dedup. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.

That topology is the evidence for the answer: A unique message ID recorded in the same transaction as the inventory update lets redelivery detect a completed effect. exercises.prompt: The network between your two datacenters goes down. CAP says you must now choose. Choose what, exactly?
choices: Between consistency, availability and partition tolerance — pick any two
Between refusing writes (staying consistent) and accepting them on both sides (staying available) — the partition isn't a choice, it's the weather
Between SQL and NoSQL
Between latency and throughput
exercises.why: A network partition prevents the two datacenters from exchanging messages and creates the condition addressed by CAP. During that interval, preserving one consistent history requires refusing operations that need cross-partition agreement. Preserving availability permits each reachable side to accept operations and requires later conflict detection and reconciliation. The system makes this choice per affected operation while coordination is unavailable.
exercises.hint: Which of the three letters did you actually get a vote on?

exercises.prompt: Match each consistency model to what it actually promises.

pairs.right: Every read sees the latest committed write, as if there were one copy
Stop writing and the copies converge — with no promise about when
You always see your own changes; other people's may lag
You never see time go backwards

exercises.why: Linearizability makes completed operations appear in one real-time order, so a read after a completed write observes that write. Eventual consistency promises convergence after writes stop without a convergence deadline. Read-your-writes ensures a client sees its own completed changes, while monotonic reads prevent that client from later observing an older version than one it has already seen. A system can select these guarantees per operation and observer.
exercises.hint: Two of these are about what *you* see; one is about everyone; one has no deadline.

exercises.prompt: A quorum system has N=5 replicas, W=3, R=3. W+R > N, so the read and write sets always overlap. Does that give you strong consistency?
choices: Yes — overlap means a read always sees the latest write
No — overlap guarantees a read *touches* a replica that saw the write, but not that it can tell which value is newest, or that a half-finished write is resolved
Yes, as long as N is odd
Only if W = N
exercises.why: Because W+R exceeds N, every successful read quorum includes at least one replica from every successful write quorum. That overlap guarantees contact with a replica that received the write, but the reader still needs a reliable version order and rules for concurrent or partially completed writes. Without a protocol that chooses one committed order and prevents later reads from returning older values, quorum overlap alone does not provide linearizability.
exercises.hint: What does the read set do with two different values it found?

exercises.prompt: Raft elects a leader by majority vote. Why isn't 'won a majority' enough on its own to make someone leader?
choices: It is enough — a majority is a majority
A majority could elect a candidate that's missing committed writes, so Raft additionally refuses to vote for anyone whose log is behind the voter's
Because elections can tie
Because the old leader might come back
exercises.why: A candidate can obtain leadership only if it receives a majority and its log is at least as up to date as each granting voter's log, compared by last-log term and then index. Committed entries are stored on a majority, and an election majority overlaps that set. Raft's voting restriction and log-matching rules use this overlap to prevent election of a leader that would discard committed entries.
exercises.hint: Two majorities of the same set always share at least one member.

exercises.prompt: Which statements describe a recoverable backup system rather than another live replica? Select all.
choices: It retains point-in-time history so yesterday's uncorrupted state remains available
Restore procedures are exercised and measured against the recovery objectives
It immediately mirrors every accidental deletion into the only remaining copy
Credentials and failure domains are separated enough that one production compromise cannot erase every recovery copy
exercises.why: A backup preserves recoverable history across production mistakes and failures. Point-in-time retention, isolated control, and tested restores provide that capability. A live replica improves availability but faithfully copies corruption and deletion, so replication alone is not recovery.
exercises.hint: Ask what happens when production correctly replicates the wrong operation.

exercises.prompt: Global dashboards are green and synthetic checks confirm telemetry is arriving. Complaints cluster on Android version 12 in Brazil. What data exposes the hidden failure?
choices: Nothing — the users are wrong
High-cardinality events sliced by app version, country, endpoint, and error, then traces from affected requests
The dashboards need a faster refresh
You need more dashboards
exercises.why: The prompt rules out a dead telemetry pipeline and supplies a cohort hidden by global aggregation. High-cardinality structured events preserve dimensions such as version and country so operators can isolate that cohort; distributed traces then reveal which request hop fails. Green global averages alone cannot show a severe failure affecting a small segment.
exercises.hint: Who chose which questions your dashboard can answer, and when?

exercises.prompt: Order a disaster-recovery exercise from business requirement to proven restore.
steps: Define the maximum tolerable data loss as the recovery point objective (RPO)
Define the maximum tolerable service restoration time as the recovery time objective (RTO)
Choose backup frequency, retention, isolation, and restore capacity that can meet both objectives
Restore into an isolated environment using documented automation
Verify integrity and application behavior against known checks
Measure achieved data loss and elapsed recovery time, then repair any gap before production depends on the claim
exercises.why: RPO and RTO are business constraints, not labels attached after choosing a backup product. A recovery design becomes a guarantee only after a realistic restore verifies data integrity and demonstrates that measured loss and restoration time satisfy those constraints.
exercises.hint: A backup that has never been restored is an untested input, not a recovery capability.

exercises.prompt: Your service calls a flaky dependency. You add retries. The dependency now goes down completely for ten minutes instead of degrading. What did the retries do?
choices: Nothing — retries are always safe
They multiplied load exactly when the dependency was weakest, turning a slowdown into a retry storm that finished it off
They fixed the problem
They caused a memory leak
exercises.why: When the dependency slows, callers time out and issue additional attempts while the original load is still present. Those attempts consume more connections, CPU, and queue capacity, creating a retry storm that can prevent recovery. Bounded attempts, exponential backoff, randomized jitter, retry budgets, and circuit breaking limit amplification; retrying a state-changing operation also requires idempotency.
exercises.hint: What does the dependency see, from every caller at once?

exercises.prompt: Complete the partition-safe write path: commits need a majority, and external effects must reject the stale leader.
exercises.why: The current-term leader commits only after a majority acknowledges, then presents its increasing fencing token to external systems. The isolated old leader lacks a quorum, so its database writes cannot commit; if an external sink ignores fencing tokens, that stale leader can still trigger duplicate or conflicting side effects outside the consensus log.
exercises.hint: Can the old leader actually *commit* anything?

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Complete the partition-safe write path: commits need a majority, and external effects must reject the stale leader.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client Write → Current Leader; Current Leader → Majority Quorum; Majority Quorum → Fenced External Sink. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The current-term leader commits only after a majority acknowledges, then presents its increasing fencing token to external systems. The isolated old leader lacks a quorum, so its database writes cannot commit; if an external sink ignores fencing tokens, that stale leader can still trigger duplicate or conflicting side effects outside the consensus log.

exercises.prompt: You're choosing consistency for a social feed's like counter — millions of writes, shown everywhere.
exercises.leftLabel: Eventual — fast, may be briefly wrong
exercises.why: A briefly stale aggregate like count usually tolerates asynchronous updates because individual likes can be merged and the display need not reflect one global order immediately. Requiring a linearizable count would coordinate writes to a highly contended item, increasing latency and reducing availability during partitions. Other operations in the same product can still require stronger guarantees, so consistency is chosen per operation.
exercises.hint: Who is harmed by a like count being two seconds stale?

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually help you debug a failure you did not predict? Select all.
choices: High-cardinality structured events you can slice by user, version, region after the fact
Distributed tracing that follows one request across every service it touched
A dashboard of average latency per service
Alerting on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency) rather than on causes (CPU)
exercises.why: Structured events with high-cardinality dimensions let operators isolate the affected users, versions, or regions after a novel failure appears. Distributed traces then show which hop delayed or failed a specific request. Symptom-based alerts detect user-visible impact without assuming a cause. A service-wide average discards distribution and cohort information, so it can hide tail latency or a failure confined to one region.
exercises.hint: Three of these preserve information. One of them destroys it on purpose.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of this tier?
choices: Distributed systems are too hard; keep everything on one machine
Global ordering, linearizability, consensus, and mutually exclusive commitments require coordination; choose them only for operations whose invariants need them
Use a database that says it's strongly consistent and stop worrying
Eventual consistency is always fine
exercises.why: Guarantees that impose one global order or one exclusive winner require coordination among failure-independent components. Linearizable writes and consensus commonly wait for quorum communication, adding latency and rejecting work without a quorum. Eventual consistency and some client-session guarantees do not require synchronous global coordination. Select each guarantee for the invariant it protects.
exercises.hint: Which guarantees require independent machines to agree before answering?

exercises.prompt: A payment worker times out, retries, and a network partition hides the current leader. Which design preserves one charge?
choices: Accept writes independently on both partition sides
Rely on average latency
Stable idempotency identity plus an authoritative quorum/fenced writer
A random key per retry
exercises.why: The stable key identifies one payment intent, while quorum-backed or fenced authority prevents two independent histories from accepting conflicting claims.
